scope: Controlled external authority and peer-reviewed source registry for THC-ENC claim-level evidence collection. Source inclusion does not approve a lesson, publish a draft, or complete independent science review.
rules: Source records identify authority and applicability; they do not create publication authorization.
Every lesson-level claim mapping must remain review-pending until independently reviewed.
Regulatory and standards sources must be rechecked at release time because requirements can change.
Project-internal source packets may guide architecture, but external source records are preferred for claim-level evidence.

sources.title: NIH Grants & Funding: Enhancing Reproducibility through Rigor and Transparency
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general evidence-discipline, reproducibility, rigor, and transparent-reporting expectations. It is not cannabis-specific and does not rank individual cultivation claims.

sources.title: Papoutsoglou et al. (2020). Enabling reusability of plant phenomic datasets with MIAPPE 1.1.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for plant-phenotyping metadata, protocol, environmental-context, and reusable dataset requirements. It is a plant phenomics standard, not a cannabis cultivation recipe.

sources.title: Livingston et al. (2023). Glandular trichome development, morphology, and maturation are influenced by plant age and genotype in high THC-containing cannabis.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis-specific trichome-development and maturation evidence. Apply within the studied genotype, tissue, age, and method boundaries.

sources.title: Postharvest Operations of Cannabis and Their Effect on Cannabinoid Content: A Review.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for drying, trimming, equilibrium moisture, sorption, curing, storage, packaging, and cannabinoid-context overview. Review-level evidence must be mapped to specific claims and not treated as universal target proof.

sources.title: Post-Harvest Operations to Generate High-Quality Medicinal Cannabis Products: A Systematic Review.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for medicinal-cannabis postharvest quality factors, moisture, light, temperature, duration, and drying-technique context. It does not establish one universal postharvest protocol.

sources.title: The influence of drying and storage conditions on the volatilome and cannabinoid content of Cannabis sativa L. inflorescences.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for controlled drying/storage comparisons and measured volatile/cannabinoid outcomes. Apply only within the tested varieties, storage conditions, and analytical methods.

sources.title: NIST: Metrological Traceability Frequently Asked Questions and NIST Policy.
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for traceability, calibration records, measurement uncertainty, measurand clarity, and fitness-for-purpose boundaries. It is not cannabis-specific and does not validate a particular device.

sources.title: NOAA NCEI: U.S. Climate Normals, 1991-2020.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for U.S. station climate-normal baselines. Normals describe historical distributions and are not crop forecasts or site-specific risk guarantees.

sources.title: USDA NRCS: Web Soil Survey.
sources.publisher: United States Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Conservation Service
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for mapped U.S. soil-resource planning information. Onsite sampling, current field conditions, drainage, contamination, and engineering constraints still require verification.

sources.title: USDA NRCS: Conservation Practice Standards.
sources.publisher: United States Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Conservation Service
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for minimum science-based conservation-practice criteria and as an index to practice-specific standards. Local Field Office Technical Guide, engineering review, law, and site conditions control implementation.

sources.title: USDA NRCS: Irrigation Water Management Conservation Practice Standard 449.
sources.publisher: United States Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Conservation Service
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for irrigation-water-management planning criteria. It is not a cannabis-specific irrigation schedule and requires local technical review.

sources.title: USDA NRCS: Irrigation System, Microirrigation Conservation Practice Standard 441.
sources.publisher: United States Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Conservation Service
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for microirrigation planning/design criteria. It does not replace local design, water-quality review, pressure testing, or crop-specific validation.

sources.title: Loreti and Perata (2020). The Many Facets of Hypoxia in Plants.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for plant oxygen sensing, hypoxia physiology, respiration constraints, waterlogging context, and plant responses to low oxygen. It is general plant physiology rather than cannabis-specific production evidence.

sources.title: Zarebanadkouki et al. (2019). Root water uptake and its pathways across the root: quantification at the cellular scale.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for apoplastic and cell-to-cell root-water transport pathways and method-aware root hydraulics. The experiment used lupin, so mechanism can inform cannabis physiology but species-specific quantitative transfer is not justified.

sources.title: Blatt (2024). A charged existence: A century of transmembrane ion transport in plants.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for plant membrane ion transport, electrochemical gradients, transport proteins, and energy coupling. It is broad plant physiology and does not establish cannabis-specific nutrient targets or transporter kinetics.

sources.title: PubChem PUG REST
sources.publisher: National Library of Medicine / National Center for Biotechnology Information
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for stable PubChem CID-based chemical identity, structure identifiers, and database-reported molecular properties. PubChem identity records do not by themselves establish cannabis-specific abundance, cultivation response, pharmacology, or health effects.

sources.title: USDA Hemp Phenotyping and Protocol Handbook, Version 4
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp-specific descriptor definitions, germplasm characterization, and measurement protocols. Preserve method/version context; descriptor definitions do not establish universal cultivation targets.

sources.title: Minimum Information About Plant Phenotyping Experiments (MIAPPE) v1.2
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for experiment, biological-material, environment, treatment, observation-variable, and data-management metadata. MIAPPE structures evidence but does not validate a biological or cultivation claim.

sources.title: USDA GRIN-Global Cannabis sativa L. taxon and germplasm records
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for accession identity, taxonomy, passport metadata, germplasm conservation context, and current availability metadata. Availability and counts are volatile and require retrieval timestamps.

sources.title: The USDA-ARS Hemp Germplasm Repository
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for institutional context on the USDA-ARS hemp germplasm program and its characterization goals. Current accession counts and availability must be refreshed from GRIN-Global.

sources.title: Toth (2022). Elucidating the Genetic Control of Qualitative Traits in Hemp
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for study-scoped hemp genetics findings including flowering-time loci and qualitative trait genetics. Preserve germplasm, population, and analysis context; do not universalize dissertation findings across all Cannabis.

sources.title: Diseases Affecting Hemp in New York (2020 Version)
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp-specific disease occurrence, prevention context, and symptom/pathogen examples documented in New York production. Geography, cultivar, season, production system, and current product registrations limit transfer.

sources.title: Fusarium vascular wilt of hemp
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp Fusarium vascular-wilt signs, soilborne-pathogen context, vascular colonization, and drainage-oriented prevention. Do not infer species identity from wilt symptoms alone.

sources.title: Scouting a hemp field for disease and insects
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for field scouting workflow, incidence/severity concepts, spatial-pattern observations, and recordkeeping. Scouting observations narrow a differential but do not independently establish pathogen identity.

sources.title: The role of weather in disease progression
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp disease-risk context involving humidity, rainfall, leaf wetness, drainage, temperature, and airflow. Weather context changes disease probability; it is not a pathogen diagnosis.

sources.title: Hop latent viroid in hemp
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for HLVd symptom variability, clean-stock/testing, sanitation, exclusion, and transmission-risk context in hemp. Symptoms alone are not diagnostic; testing and production-context review remain necessary.

sources.title: Abiotic vs. biotic issues in hemp fields
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for pattern-based distinction between abiotic and biotic stress and hemp-specific examples of water, temperature, nutrient, wind, and root-disease symptoms. Pattern recognition is differential evidence, not proof of cause.

sources.title: Dowling et al. (2024). A FLOWERING LOCUS T ortholog is associated with photoperiod-insensitive flowering in hemp (Cannabis sativa L.).
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis/hemp photoperiod sensitivity, photoperiod-insensitive flowering, and CsFT1-associated genetic evidence. Do not convert the studied loci or germplasm into universal flowering schedules or training-tolerance claims.

sources.title: Buirs, Lung, and Punja (2025). The epidemiology and management of Botrytis cinerea causing bud rot on greenhouse cultivated cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.).
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for greenhouse cannabis Botrytis epidemiology, inflorescence microclimate, and tested air-circulation effects. Treatment outcomes are facility-, genotype-, disease-, and protocol-specific and do not define a universal fan-speed target.

sources.title: Omary, Matosevich, and Efroni (2023). Systemic control of plant regeneration and wound repair.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general plant wound/regeneration signaling, systemic coordination, auxin, sugars, and physiological-state context. It is not cannabis-specific and does not establish cannabis recovery intervals.

sources.title: Nimmala, Ross, and Foroutan (2024). Cannabis pollen dispersal across the United States.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for meteorology-dependent windborne cannabis/hemp pollen transport modeling and spatial/seasonal dispersal context. Atmospheric transport and deposition do not equal successful fertilization and do not create a universal safe isolation distance.

sources.title: Punja and Holmes (2020). Hermaphroditism in Marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) Inflorescences—Impact on Floral Morphology, Seed Formation, Progeny Sex Ratios, and Genetic Variation.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis floral morphology, anther/pollen observations, pollen germination, pollen-tube growth on receptive stigmas, and seed formation in the studied material. Do not infer a universal stigma-receptivity day count across cultivars.

sources.title: Wizenberg, Weis, and Campbell (2020). Comparing methods for controlled capture and quantification of pollen in Cannabis sativa.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis-specific pollen capture, controlled handling, and pollen quantification methods. Method performance does not by itself prove parentage or containment in another facility or field.

sources.title: Jacuńska et al. (2026). Antioxidant Capacity of Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) Leaves and Inflorescences.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cultivar- and tissue-specific ABTS, DPPH, FRAP, and total-phenolic measurements in hemp extracts. In-vitro antioxidant assays do not prove intact-plant stress tolerance or human clinical efficacy.

sources.title: Chen et al. (2024). Feature-Based Molecular Network-Assisted Cannabinoid and Flavonoid Profiling of Cannabis sativa Leaves and Their Antioxidant Properties.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis leaf metabolite profiling and the study's in-vitro antioxidant assay relationships. Geographic/sample associations and extract assays must remain within the sampled materials and methods.

sources.title: Galic et al. (2022). Effects of Cold Temperature and Acclimation on Cold Tolerance and Cannabinoid Profiles of Cannabis sativa L. (Hemp).
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cultivar-, age-, acclimation-, and treatment-specific hemp cold-response evidence including chlorophyll fluorescence, electrolyte leakage, biomass, and cannabinoid measurements. Experimental temperatures are not universal injury thresholds.

sources.title: Corredor-Perilla, Kwon, and Park (2025). Elevated relative humidity significantly decreases cannabinoid concentrations while delaying flowering development in Cannabis sativa L.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the tested CBD-dominant genotype under the study's low-versus-very-high canopy RH treatments. Do not convert the treatment ranges into universal cannabis VPD/RH targets or injury thresholds.

sources.title: Garcia-de Heer, Kretzschmar, and Mieog (2026). Harnessing Sex Reversion via Chemical Intervention in Cannabis sativa L.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis-specific hormone-pathway manipulation of sex expression. Treatment effects are genotype-, chemical-, dose-, stage-, and protocol-specific and do not establish lawful production use or universal hormone control of sex.

sources.title: Sands et al. (2023). Hormonal control of promoter activities of Cannabis sativa prenyltransferase 1 and 4 and salicylic acid mediated regulation of cannabinoid biosynthesis.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis-specific promoter/hormone signaling and salicylic-acid-associated cannabinoid-pathway evidence. Promoter or metabolite responses do not establish disease control, yield benefit, or universal elicitor protocols.

sources.title: Wee et al. (2025). Same, yet different: towards understanding nutrient use in hemp- and drug-type Cannabis.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis/hemp nutrient acquisition, utilization, source-sink, domestication, nitrogen, and phosphorus context. It does not establish universal micronutrient tissue standards or deficiency thresholds.

sources.title: Schappe, Ritchie, and Thiessen (2020). First Report of Serratia marcescens Causing a Leaf Spot Disease on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa).
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for a confirmed bacterial hemp leaf-spot pathosystem with pathogenicity evidence. A single disease report does not imply that all angular or necrotic leaf spots are bacterial or caused by Serratia.

sources.title: Punja et al. (2024). Challenges to Cannabis sativa Production from Pathogens and Microbes—The Role of Molecular Diagnostics and Bioinformatics.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis/hemp pathogen diversity, molecular diagnostics, sequencing, viroid/virus detection, and causal-inference limits. Detection alone does not prove that an organism caused a specific symptom.

sources.title: Han et al. (2026). Beet Curly Top Virus Genetic Diversity, Impact on Cannabinoids, Potential Seed Transmission, and Vector Biology in Hemp.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp BCTV diversity, infection effects, seed-associated detection/grow-out evidence, and vector biology in the studied systems. Genotype-specific effects and low-frequency transmission observations should not be universalized.

sources.title: Acquaah — Principles of Plant Genetics and Breeding, 3rd Edition.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for plant-breeding objectives, target trait definition, selection methods, experimental design, cultivar development, and germplasm use. It is general plant breeding rather than Cannabis-specific evidence.

sources.title: Flajšman, Slapnik, and Murovec (2021). Production of Feminized Seeds of High CBD Cannabis sativa L. by Manipulation of Sex Expression and Its Application to Breeding.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for Cannabis-specific induced male flowering on female plants, pollen functionality, seed production, and breeding context. Treatment response is genotype-, method-, stage-, and protocol-specific and does not constitute a universal production recipe.

sources.title: Rodriguez-Morrison, Llewellyn, and Zheng (2021). Cannabis Yield, Potency, and Leaf Photosynthesis Respond Differently to Increasing Light Levels in an Indoor Environment.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for indoor drug-type cannabis responses to canopy PPFD, leaf photosynthesis, morphology, yield, and quality under the tested environment. The tested range does not define a universal photoinhibition threshold across genotypes or production systems.

sources.title: Jost et al. (2025). Sink strength, nutrient allocation, cannabinoid yield, and associated transcript profiles vary in two drug-type Cannabis chemovars.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for Cannabis-specific source-sink allocation, nutrient distribution, cannabinoid yield, and chemovar-dependent transcript/metabolite context. Findings from two chemovars should not be generalized into universal allocation rules.

sources.title: Preventing and Managing Plant Diseases — Phytotoxicity.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for defining phytotoxicity, nontarget chemical injury, exposure pathways, symptom overlap, and the need to distinguish chemical injury from other abiotic and biotic disorders. Current product labels and jurisdictional rules still control real-world chemical use.

sources.title: Bedding Plant Diseases — Phytotoxicity and disease-prevention guidance.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for greenhouse phytotoxicity symptom patterns, pesticide-related injury context, sanitation, and overlap with disease/overfertilization problems. It is not Cannabis-specific and does not authorize any product or application.

sources.title: Corn Earworm — Hemp.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp-specific corn-earworm identification, flower/seed feeding, scouting, and regional pest context. Regional occurrence and management thresholds do not transfer universally across cannabis systems.

sources.title: Cleaning and Disinfecting the Greenhouse.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cleaning-before-disinfection, organic-matter interference, surface cleanability, container/tool sanitation, and greenhouse hygiene. Product labels and current safety/legal requirements govern disinfectant use.

sources.title: Pythium.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for greenhouse Pythium biology, water/reservoir/hydroponic pathways, sanitation, and irrigation-system disease context. It is general horticultural guidance and does not prove Pythium in a cannabis crop without diagnosis.

sources.title: Root Diseases Prevalent in Industrial Hemp — Pythium root rot guidance.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp-specific Pythium root-rot symptoms, excess-moisture risk, water movement, and field/greenhouse prevention context. Symptom overlap requires diagnostic confirmation.

sources.title: Architecture and Florogenesis in Female Cannabis sativa Plants
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for female cannabis phytomer, branching, solitary-flower, photoperiod, and inflorescence-architecture observations in the studied genotypes and controlled conditions. Do not generalize numerical architecture responses as universal cultivar targets.

sources.title: Plant architecture manipulation increases cannabinoid standardization in drug-type medical cannabis
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for experimentally observed effects of architecture-modulation treatments on morphology and spatial cannabinoid standardization in two medical-cannabis genotypes. Treatment responses were genotype- and cannabinoid-specific and are not universal pruning prescriptions.
sources.reviewUse: claim-level cannabis architecture and uniformity source

sources.title: Too Dense or Not Too Dense: Higher Planting Density Reduces Cannabinoid Uniformity but Increases Yield/Area in Drug-Type Medical Cannabis
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the studied density-by-architecture effects on yield per plant, yield per area, lower-canopy conditions, and spatial cannabinoid uniformity. Do not convert the tested densities into universal recommendations.
sources.reviewUse: claim-level cannabis density and canopy source

sources.title: Impact of Harvest Time and Pruning Technique on Total CBD Concentration and Yield of Medicinal Cannabis
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the studied pruning-treatment effects on biomass, CBD/CBDA concentration, and total CBD yield. Results depend on the tested cultivar, harvest timing, pruning definitions, and production system.

sources.title: The curious origins of a high-stress training technique mainlining: its molecular, biochemical, and agronomic perspectives for the cultivation of Cannabis sativa
sources.useAndLimitations: Use as a review of mainlining terminology, proposed mechanisms, and research gaps. The review explicitly notes limited scientific validation and lack of standardized protocols; it should not be treated as direct proof of a universal mainlining response.

sources.title: Strigolactones and Shoot Branching: What Is the Real Hormone and How Does It Work?
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general plant shoot-branching mechanisms involving axillary buds, strigolactones, auxin, cytokinin, nutritional signals, and bud outgrowth. These mechanisms are not direct cannabis-specific dose or timing evidence.

sources.title: Shape Matters: Plant Architecture Affects Chemical Uniformity in Large-Size Medical Cannabis Plants
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for experimentally observed relationships among large-plant architecture, vertical light gradients, pruning/defoliation treatments, biomass, and spatial cannabinoid uniformity in the studied cultivar and greenhouse system. Do not generalize the tested architecture treatments or numerical outcomes as universal canopy prescriptions.
sources.reviewUse: claim-level cannabis canopy and architecture source

sources.title: Is Twelve Hours Really the Optimum Photoperiod for Promoting Flowering in Indoor-Grown Cultivars of Cannabis sativa?
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cultivar-dependent flowering-initiation and early-flower responses under 12–15 h photoperiods in ten indoor drug-type cultivars. Do not convert tested responses into a universal critical photoperiod or flowering schedule.

sources.title: Photoperiodic Flowering Response of Essential Oil, Grain, and Fiber Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) Cultivars
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cultivar-specific photoperiod thresholds, flowering delay, extension growth, and day-neutral behavior across the tested hemp cultivars. Critical photoperiods depend on cultivar, source, endpoint, and environment.

sources.title: Development and Optimization of a Germination Assay and Long-Term Storage for Cannabis sativa Pollen
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis pollen developmental stage, in-vitro germination methodology, and the specific tested cryopreservation approach. Do not generalize the protocol into indefinite viability under ordinary freezer storage.
sources.reviewUse: claim-level cannabis pollen germination and storage source

sources.title: Methods for characterizing pollen fitness in Cannabis sativa L.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for distinguishing pollen non-abortion staining from in-vitro germination/viability and for method-dependent pollen-fitness estimates. Laboratory fitness proxies do not equal whole-plant fertilization success.

sources.title: Fertilization Following Pollination Predominantly Decreases Phytocannabinoids Accumulation and Alters the Accumulation of Terpenoids in Cannabis Inflorescences
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct cannabis evidence comparing fertilized and unfertilized inflorescences and subsequent cannabinoid/terpenoid accumulation. Magnitudes and directions remain chemovar-, compound-, tissue-, and protocol-dependent.

sources.title: Inflorescence development in female cannabis plants is mediated by photoperiod and gibberellin
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the studied two-phase short-day elongation/condensation response, continuous short-day requirement, and long-day reversion of inflorescence architecture. Exact day counts and hormone responses were observed in a limited cultivar context and are not universal cannabis schedules.

sources.title: Hermaphroditism in Cannabis sativa L.: Impacts, Inducers, and Industry Implications
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the current synthesis of genetic, hormonal, developmental, treatment, and environmental contributors to cannabis sex-expression instability. Review evidence supports a context-dependent model, not one universal environmental trigger threshold.

sources.title: Determination of Germination and Emergence Performance of Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) Seeds at Different Maturity Stages
sources.publisher: Turkish Journal of Agriculture - Food Science and Technology
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct comparison of mature, semi-mature, and immature hemp seed germination/emergence performance and for evidence that seed maturity is heterogeneous. Do not convert the study into a universal harvest percentage, color rule, or days-after-pollination threshold.

sources.title: Analysis of cannabinoids in laser-microdissected trichomes of medicinal Cannabis sativa using LCMS and cryogenic NMR
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct cannabinoid detection in laser-microdissected capitate-sessile and capitate-stalked trichome fractions and for trichome distribution/density observations. Small isolated fractions and gland classes do not by themselves quantify whole-flower contribution.

sources.title: A polarized supercell produces specialized metabolites in cannabis trichomes
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for ultra-rapid cryofixation/electron-microscopy evidence of polarized cannabis secretory cells, plastid/ER/plasma-membrane contacts, pathway localization, and THCAS localization at the extracellular cavity-facing wall. Proposed trafficking models should remain distinguished from directly observed localization.

sources.title: The hexanoyl-CoA precursor for cannabinoid biosynthesis is formed by an acyl-activating enzyme in Cannabis sativa trichomes
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct detection of hexanoyl-CoA in cannabis tissues, trichome-enriched CsAAE1 expression, in-vitro acyl-activating activity, and precursor-pathway context. The upstream origin of hexanoate and intact-plant flux control remain incompletely resolved.

sources.title: Identification of olivetolic acid cyclase from Cannabis sativa reveals a unique catalytic route to plant polyketides
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct biochemical evidence that cannabis tetraketide synthase requires olivetolic acid cyclase to form olivetolic acid and for trichome-enriched pathway context. Purified-enzyme capability does not by itself establish intact-plant flux control.

sources.title: Prenylation of olivetolate by a hemp transferase yields cannabigerolic acid, the precursor of tetrahydrocannabinol
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct enzyme evidence that olivetolic acid and GPP can be converted to CBGA by cannabis/hemp prenyltransferase activity. Later pathway work refines enzyme identity; this early study does not alone establish which prenyltransferase dominates every genotype.

sources.title: The gene controlling marijuana psychoactivity: molecular cloning and heterologous expression of tetrahydrocannabinolic acid synthase from Cannabis sativa L.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct cloning, heterologous-expression, biochemical, and FAD-dependent evidence that THCA synthase catalyzes oxidative cyclization of CBGA to THCA. Enzyme identity does not by itself determine whole-plant THCA concentration.

sources.title: Cannabidiolic-acid synthase, the chemotype-determining enzyme in the fiber-type Cannabis sativa
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for recombinant CBDAS evidence converting CBGA to CBDA and for biochemical characterization of CBDAS. Genotype does not uniquely determine absolute crop concentration without expression, precursor, environment, sampling, and analytical context.

sources.title: A physical and genetic map of Cannabis sativa identifies extensive rearrangements at the THC/CBD acid synthase loci
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabinoid synthase-locus structural complexity, aromatic prenyltransferase mapping, CBCAS gene identification, and catalytic characterization. Results derive from specific drug/hemp genomes and a defined cross; locus architecture and marker performance require population-aware interpretation.

sources.title: Complex Patterns of Cannabinoid Alkyl Side-Chain Inheritance in Cannabis
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for F2 evidence that alkyl side-chain composition shows complex inheritance involving linkage, epistasis, dominance, and lineage-specific effects. Do not reduce propyl/pentyl cannabinoid inheritance to a simple universal single-locus rule.

sources.title: Luo et al. (2019). Complete biosynthesis of cannabinoids and their unnatural analogues in yeast.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for reconstructed cannabinoid biosynthesis, major cannabinoid-acid pathways, CBGA-forming prenyltransferase function, and alternate precursor use. Engineered-yeast flux and yields are not cannabis cultivation targets.

sources.title: Wang et al. (2016). Decarboxylation Study of Acidic Cannabinoids.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for controlled analytical evidence on time- and temperature-dependent decarboxylation of acidic cannabinoids. The tested analytical conditions do not define a universal processing recipe for plant material.

sources.title: Milay et al. (2020). Metabolic Profiling of Cannabis Secondary Metabolites for Evaluation of Optimal Postharvest Storage Conditions.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for measured postharvest cannabinoid and terpenoid changes under defined storage conditions. Apply only within the tested chemovars, sample forms, temperatures, durations, and analytical methods.

sources.title: Namdar et al. (2018). Variation in the compositions of cannabinoids and terpenoids in Cannabis sativa derived from inflorescence position along the stem and extraction methods.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for position-dependent and method-dependent variation in measured cannabis chemistry. The study supports position-defined sampling but does not establish one universal spatial gradient for all genotypes or production systems.

sources.title: Sarma et al. (2020). Cannabis Inflorescence for Medical Purposes: USP Considerations for Quality Attributes.
sources.publisher: Journal of Natural Products / United States Pharmacopeia expert panel
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis inflorescence identity, representative sampling, analytical quality attributes, and limits of inferring whole-batch composition from a submitted sample. It is a quality-framework review, not a universal jurisdictional release standard.

sources.title: Booth, Page, and Bohlmann (2017). Terpene synthases from Cannabis sativa.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis trichome terpene-pathway transcriptomics and functional characterization of mono- and sesquiterpene synthases. Enzyme products and one cultivar's profiles do not establish universal abundance or sensory effects.

sources.title: Allen et al. (2019). Genomic characterization of the complete terpene synthase gene family from Cannabis sativa.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis TPS gene-family diversity, genomic context, tissue expression, and commercial terpene-profile variation. Annotation and expression do not by themselves establish enzyme product or human effect.

sources.title: Oswald et al. (2021). Identification of a New Family of Prenylated Volatile Sulfur Compounds in Cannabis Revealed by Comprehensive Two-Dimensional Gas Chromatography.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for prenylated volatile sulfur compounds and their association with skunk-like cannabis aroma under the tested samples and methods. Odor contribution does not establish quality, safety, or health effect.

sources.title: Oswald et al. (2023). Minor, Nonterpenoid Volatile Compounds Drive the Aroma Differences of Exotic Cannabis.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for evidence that low-abundance nonterpenoid volatiles can contribute strongly to cannabis aroma differences. The studied commercial samples do not establish universal sensory markers or cultivar identity.

sources.title: Spadafora et al. (2024). The influence of drying and storage conditions on the volatilome and cannabinoid content of Cannabis sativa L. inflorescences.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for drying- and storage-dependent changes in cannabis volatile and cannabinoid profiles. Results are method-, genotype-, and condition-specific and do not define one universal drying or storage protocol.

sources.title: MacLaughlin and MacDonald (2024). Is nitrogen-modified atmosphere packaging a tool for retention of volatile terpenes and cannabinoids in stored Cannabis sativa inflorescence?
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for controlled comparison of modified-atmosphere packaging and compound retention across tested chemovars and storage times. It does not establish a universal packaging advantage.

sources.title: Shapira et al. (2019). Tandem Mass Spectrometric Quantification of 93 Terpenoids in Cannabis Using Static Headspace Injections.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for validated cannabis terpenoid quantification and evidence that sample preparation can materially change measured terpene fingerprints. Method performance does not eliminate biological sampling variation.

sources.title: Smith et al. (2022). The phytochemical diversity of commercial Cannabis in the United States.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for large-scale evidence that commercial labels such as Indica/Hybrid/Sativa do not consistently align with measured cannabinoid/terpene chemistry. The dataset represents participating U.S. markets and labs rather than all cannabis worldwide.

sources.title: Finlay et al. (2020). Terpenoids From Cannabis Do Not Mediate an Entourage Effect by Acting at Cannabinoid Receptors.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct receptor-level tests of selected terpenes alone and with cannabinoid ligands. Negative CB1/CB2 findings do not rule out every possible pharmacokinetic, sensory, or non-cannabinoid-receptor interaction.

sources.title: Spindle et al. (2024). Vaporized D-limonene selectively mitigates the acute anxiogenic effects of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol in healthy adults who intermittently use cannabis.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for a specific randomized human THC-plus-D-limonene interaction under tested doses and route. It does not establish broad entourage synergy across terpenes, cannabinoids, products, or clinical outcomes.

sources.title: Choi et al. (2004). NMR assignments of the major cannabinoids and cannabiflavonoids isolated from flowers of Cannabis sativa.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct structural identification of cannflavin A and cannflavin B among isolated cannabis flower constituents. Compound identification does not establish abundance, cultivation response, antioxidant effect, or clinical benefit.

sources.title: Gagalova et al. (2024). Leaf pigmentation in Cannabis sativa: Characterization of anthocyanin biosynthesis in colorful Cannabis varieties.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis anthocyanin diversity, pigmentation-associated metabolites, and expression of flavonoid-pathway genes in studied varieties. Leaf color evidence does not establish flower chemotype, potency, or stress tolerance.

sources.title: Diagnosing a Plant Problem 101
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for progression, spatial pattern, cultural history, biotic-versus-abiotic differential reasoning, and the recommendation to confirm uncertain diagnoses with representative samples or a diagnostic clinic. It is general plant guidance, not cannabis-specific proof of any symptom cause.

sources.title: Response of Medical Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) to Nitrogen Supply Under Long Photoperiod
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct cannabis nitrogen-supply effects on growth, physiology, chlorophyll-related traits, mineral nutrition, and cannabinoid response in the tested genotype/system. Treatment values are not universal deficiency or toxicity thresholds.

sources.title: The Highs and Lows of P Supply in Medical Cannabis: Effects on Cannabinoids, the Ionome, and Morpho-Physiology
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct cannabis phosphorus-supply effects on morphology, physiology, root-zone pH, ionomics, and cannabinoid outcomes. Tested supply levels do not define universal cannabis P targets or symptom thresholds.

sources.title: Response of Medical Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) Genotypes to K Supply Under Long Photoperiod
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for genotype- and potassium-supply-dependent cannabis morphology, physiology, ionomic, and growth responses. The tested genotypes and K levels do not establish a universal visual deficiency key or target range.

sources.title: Photosynthetic response of Cannabis sativa L. to variations in photosynthetic photon flux densities, temperature and CO2 conditions
sources.publisher: Physiology and Molecular Biology of Plants
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct cannabis gas-exchange and water-use responses across controlled PPFD, temperature, and CO2 treatments. The experiment does not define universal injury thresholds or environmental setpoints for all genotypes and production systems.

sources.title: Aquaponic and Hydroponic Solutions Modulate NaCl-Induced Stress in Drug-Type Cannabis sativa L.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct drug-type cannabis NaCl-stress evidence in controlled aquaponic and hydroponic solutions, including growth, physiology, yield, and cannabinoid responses. Tested NaCl concentrations and system effects must not be generalized as universal salinity thresholds.

sources.title: A Water Quality Toolkit for Greenhouse and Nursery Production
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for distinguishing water pH, alkalinity, hardness, EC/TDS, calibration/testing, and recordkeeping in greenhouse/nursery production. Screening ranges are general horticultural guidance and are not universal cannabis injury limits.

sources.title: Edema Of Geranium
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the established greenhouse water-uptake-versus-transpiration mechanism of edema and its association with wet roots, high humidity, low light, cool air, and poor ventilation. It is cross-species guidance and must not be treated as cannabis-specific diagnostic proof.

sources.title: Plant Sampling
sources.publisher: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Plant Disease Diagnostic Lab
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for representative diagnostic sampling, inclusion of roots and multiple symptom stages, healthy/symptomatic comparisons, photographs, and transition tissue. Sampling guidance improves diagnostic evidence but does not determine causation by itself.

sources.title: Arthropod and mollusk pests of hemp, Cannabis sativa, and their indoor management plan in Florida
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for documented hemp arthropod/mollusk diversity, diagnostic keys, pest-potential categories, and indoor IPM context. Florida occurrence and proposed management context do not establish universal pest prevalence, thresholds, or pesticide recommendations.

sources.title: Developing Insect Pest Management Systems for Hemp in the United States: A Work in Progress
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for major U.S. hemp arthropod pest identity, production-system context, known injury, and explicit knowledge gaps. The review predates newer pest research and does not establish universal action thresholds.

sources.title: Biology and management of hemp russet mite (Acari: Eriophyidae)
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct hemp-russet-mite biology, injury, sampling/management research, and documented knowledge gaps. Crop-damage quantification and universal thresholds remain incomplete.

sources.title: Life table analyses and feeding behaviors of cannabis aphid, cotton aphid, and green peach aphid on industrial hemp
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct host-suitability and feeding comparisons among three aphid species on the tested hemp cultivar. Results are cultivar- and experiment-specific and do not establish universal field abundance or virus risk.

sources.title: Lettuce Chlorosis Virus Disease: A New Threat to Cannabis Production
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct evidence of lettuce chlorosis virus infection in cannabis and Bemisia tabaci transmission under the studied conditions. Vector presence alone does not prove infection or establish field disease probability.

sources.title: Cannabis sativa as a Host of Rice Root Aphid in North America
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct North American evidence that indoor Cannabis can host rice root aphid, including root association and alate dispersal context. Quantitative crop-loss relationships and universal action thresholds are not established.

sources.title: Interactions of beet leafhopper, vector of beet curly top virus, and hemp in New Mexico
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct hemp field/choice-test evidence involving beet leafhopper abundance, hemp host interaction, and BCTV infection in New Mexico. Regional abundance does not define universal disease probability or treatment thresholds.

sources.title: Establishing Action Thresholds
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for quantitative action-threshold concepts, crop-value context, consistent monitoring, and local threshold development. Examples are ornamental-production guidance and are not cannabis-specific thresholds.

sources.title: Using Integrated Pest Management in Greenhouses and Herbaceous Nurseries
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for greenhouse scouting, sticky cards, visual inspection, life-stage records, sanitation, exclusion, and integration of cultural/biological/physical controls. Product recommendations require current label and crop/site review and are not imported into the encyclopedia.

sources.title: Starting a Biological Control Program for Greenhouse Insect and Mite Pests
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for target-specific natural-enemy planning, residue-history review, environmental fit, scouting, and compatibility concepts. It is greenhouse guidance rather than cannabis-specific efficacy evidence.

sources.title: Punja et al. (2019). Pathogens and Molds Affecting Production and Quality of Cannabis sativa L.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis-specific observations on powdery mildew, root pathogens including Pythium, endophytic and airborne fungi, postharvest molds, propagation-mediated spread, and wound-associated establishment. Multi-year production observations support organism and pathway context but do not create universal incidence, severity, or treatment thresholds.

sources.title: Gwinn et al. (2023). Fungal and mycotoxin contaminants in cannabis and hemp flowers: implications for consumer health and directions for further research.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis/hemp floral mycobiome, postharvest fungal contamination, water-activity context, toxigenic genera, analytical methods, and the distinction between fungal detection and demonstrated mycotoxin production. Do not infer that detection of a potentially toxigenic fungus proves a mycotoxin is present.
sources.reviewUse: claim-level postharvest fungal and mycotoxin source

sources.title: Punja et al. (2025). Transmission, Spread, Longevity and Management of Hop Latent Viroid, a Widespread and Destructive Pathogen Affecting Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) Plants in North America.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for direct cannabis HLVd evidence involving asymptomatic stock plants, vegetative cuttings, recirculated nutrient solution, root infection, infectious sap, tissue movement over time, and persistence in plant material. Detection and transmission results are study-specific and do not define a universal sanitation or sampling interval.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp disease-survey observations including Rhizoctonia root/crown disease and symptom/sign descriptions supported by microscopy and sequence-based identification. Survey prevalence and regional observations must not be generalized as universal cannabis incidence.

sources.title: Yang, Justice, and Colburn (2023). First Report of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum Causing Stem Canker on Industrial Hemp in South Carolina, U.S.A.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for a confirmed Sclerotinia sclerotiorum hemp stem-canker pathosystem and associated signs in the reported production context. A first report establishes host-pathogen capability, not universal prevalence, severity, or management thresholds.

sources.title: Genetic Mapping, Identification, and Characterization of a Candidate Susceptibility Gene for Powdery Mildew in Cannabis sativa.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for experimentally measured variation in cannabis powdery-mildew susceptibility and mapped candidate susceptibility genetics in the studied populations. Resistance observed in specific parents or progeny is not a universal cultivar rating or guarantee of field resistance.

sources.title: Francl (2001). The Disease Triangle: A plant pathological paradigm revisited.
sources.publisher: The Plant Health Instructor / American Phytopathological Society
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the foundational plant-pathology model that disease requires interaction among a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen, and a favorable environment, with time and human activity as useful extensions. The model organizes causal reasoning but does not identify a pathogen or quantify disease risk by itself.

sources.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Principles
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for IPM prevention, monitoring, identification, action-threshold, and control hierarchy concepts. It does not create cannabis-specific economic thresholds, pesticide permissions, or efficacy claims.

sources.title: Integrated Pest Management of Hemp in Virginia
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp-specific IPM, incoming-plant inspection/quarantine, pest monitoring, and the limited state of economic thresholds. Regional and regulatory context limits transfer.

sources.title: Cleaning and Disinfecting the Greenhouse
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for greenhouse cleaning versus disinfection, surface preparation, sanitation workflow, and contact-time concepts. Product labels and material compatibility remain controlling.

sources.title: Assessing the Risk of Disease in Greenhouses
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for clean stock, quarantine, propagation separation, structural risk, and disease-prevention assessment. It is general greenhouse guidance, not cannabis-specific proof.

sources.title: Prevention and Management of Soilborne Diseases of Ornamental Plants and Vegetables in the Greenhouse
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for sanitation, clean containers/media, water, and soilborne-disease prevention concepts. Crop and product recommendations require bounded transfer.

sources.title: Exclusion Methods for Managing Greenhouse Vegetable Pests
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for screening, structural exclusion, double-door entry, and airflow tradeoffs. Screen specification and performance are pest-, structure-, and climate-specific.

sources.title: IPM Scouting and Decision Making
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for systematic scouting routes, sticky cards, plant inspection, records, treatment evaluation, and context-dependent thresholds. It does not establish universal cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Plant Diagnostic Clinic: Guidelines for Collecting and Submitting Samples
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for representative diagnostic samples, symptom stages, transition tissue, photographs, and submission context. Sampling quality does not by itself establish causation.

sources.title: Introduction to Pesticide Labels
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the legal role of pesticide labeling and directions for use. Current registration, crop/site language, state rules, worker protection, and label text control actual use.

sources.title: Corrective and Preventive Actions (CAPA), Quality System Inspection Technique
sources.useAndLimitations: Use as a transferable quality-system framework for investigation, corrective/preventive action, effectiveness verification, and documentation. It is not cannabis-cultivation regulation.

sources.title: United States-Canada Greenhouse-Grown Plant Certification Program Technical Requirements
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for systems audits, surveillance, objective evidence, integrated pest-risk measures, and corrective measures in greenhouse facilities. Program scope does not automatically apply to cannabis operations.

sources.title: Phenotypic plasticity influences the success of clonal propagation in industrial pharmaceutical Cannabis sativa
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis-specific mother-plant and stem-cutting propagation responses, including cultivar and treatment effects. Results are cultivar-, environment-, and protocol-specific and do not define universal rooting performance or production recipes.

sources.title: Evaluation of substrate composition and exogenous hormone application on vegetative propagule rooting success of essential oil hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for hemp cutting substrate and exogenous hormone effects on rooting metrics. Responses are cultivar-, substrate-, dose-, and protocol-specific and do not establish a universal medium, hormone dose, or rooting standard.

sources.title: Variables Affecting Shoot Growth and Plantlet Recovery in Tissue Cultures of Drug-Type Cannabis sativa L.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis-specific explant contamination, genotype effects, culture-media response, rooting, and acclimatization. Outcomes are genotype- and protocol-dependent and should not be generalized as a universal tissue-culture formula.

sources.title: Genetic Evaluation of In Vitro Micropropagated and Regenerated Plants of Cannabis sativa L. Using SSR Molecular Markers
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for genetic-stability observations in tested micropropagated and regenerated cannabis material. SSR similarity in studied material does not prove complete genomic or epigenomic identity across all cultivars, passages, regeneration routes, or laboratories.

sources.title: Micropropagation of Cannabis sativa: genetic and epigenetic stability assessment over multiple generations
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for multi-generation cannabis micropropagation stability observations in the studied lines and methods. Stability findings remain genotype-, passage-, assay-, and protocol-specific and do not guarantee absence of somatic or epigenetic change in every clonal system.

sources.title: Efficient propagation protocol and genetic similarity assessment of medicinal cannabis based on photoautotrophic micropropagation
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis photoautotrophic micropropagation, plantlet production, acclimatization, and genetic-similarity observations under the reported protocol. Results are genotype-, equipment-, vessel-, environment-, and method-specific.

sources.title: Molecular and physiological control of adventitious rooting in cuttings: phytohormone action meets resource allocation
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general plant mechanisms of cutting wound response, auxin signaling, resource allocation, and adventitious-root formation. It supports mechanism transfer only and is not cannabis-specific evidence for dose, timing, or rooting performance.

sources.title: Adventitious Roots and Lateral Roots: Similarities and Differences
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for foundational developmental distinctions and shared regulatory features of adventitious versus lateral roots. The review is cross-species and should not be used to infer cannabis-specific rooting thresholds.

sources.title: Cryopreservation of Shoot Tips of Elite Cultivars of Cannabis sativa L. by Droplet Vitrification
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for demonstrated cannabis shoot-tip cryopreservation and recovery under the reported droplet-vitrification protocol. It does not establish a universal cryopreservation recipe, survival rate, or safety procedure for all genotypes or facilities.

sources.title: Villard et al. (2026). Resurrected Ancestral Cannabis Enzymes Unveil the Origin and Functional Evolution of Cannabinoid Synthases.
aliases: Resurrected Ancestral Cannabis Enzymes Unveil the Origin and Functional Evolution of Cannabinoid Synthases (2025/2026 publication record). Ancestral oxidocyclase reconstruction found early promiscuous enzymes capable of producing THCA, CBDA, and CBCA, supporting an evolutionary model of later subfunctionalization.
Resurrected Ancestral Cannabis Enzymes Unveil the Origin and Functional Evolution of Cannabinoid Synthases
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for ancestral-sequence reconstruction and functional-evolution evidence showing early cannabinoid oxidocyclase promiscuity and later specialization. Ancestral-enzyme reconstruction does not by itself establish extant cultivar chemotype, field performance, or universal biosynthetic flux.

sources.title: Llewellyn et al. (2023). Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies.
aliases: Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies (Plants, 2023). Demonstrates system- and element-specific symptomology rather than a universal photo diagnosis.
Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis-specific single-element deficiency symptom progression, tissue analysis, yield effects, and the warning that visual symptoms and tissue concentrations do not always align. Results are cultivar-, hydroponic-system-, stage-, treatment-, and environment-specific and do not create universal visual-diagnosis rules.

sources.title: Chandra et al. (2011). Photosynthetic response of Cannabis sativa L., an important medicinal plant, to elevated levels of CO2.
sources.publisher: Physiology and Molecular Biology of Plants
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cannabis leaf gas-exchange responses to the tested elevated CO2 concentrations in four studied varieties. Short-term leaf photosynthesis and water-use responses do not establish universal whole-crop yield, quality, economic, or facility-control targets.

sources.title: NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards: Carbon Dioxide
sources.publisher: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for NIOSH carbon-dioxide hazard identity, REL/ST exposure limits, IDLH concentration, symptoms, measurement-method references, and occupational-safety context. Occupational exposure limits are not crop-production setpoints and do not design a cultivation CO2 system.

sources.title: Llewellyn et al. (2022). Indoor grown cannabis yield increased proportionally with light intensity, but ultraviolet radiation did not affect yield or cannabinoid content.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for responses of the tested indoor cannabis genotype to 600, 800, and 1,000 µmol m−2 s−1 canopy PPFD and the reported UVA/UVB treatments. The tested range and genotype do not define a universal safe-light ceiling, photoinhibition threshold, or UV response.

sources.title: Zhang et al. (2021). Photoperiodic Flowering Response of Essential Oil, Grain, and Fiber Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) Cultivars.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for cultivar-specific hemp flowering responses across tested 12–18 h controlled photoperiods, field day length, critical-photoperiod differences, and biologically effective twilight observations. The tested hemp cultivars and environments do not establish a universal critical photoperiod for all cannabis germplasm.

sources.title: Dang, Muthu Arachchige, and Campbell (2022). Optimizing Photoperiod Switch to Maximize Floral Biomass and Cannabinoid Yield in Cannabis sativa L.: A Meta-Analytic Quantile Regression Approach.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the reviewed relationship between duration of long-day vegetative exposure, photoperiod switching, floral biomass, and cannabinoid concentration across the included studies. Meta-analytic optima reflect the included literature and methods and are not universal cultivar recipes or critical-photoperiod thresholds.

sources.title: Saloner and Bernstein (2020). Response of Medical Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) to Nitrogen Supply Under Long Photoperiod.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for measured vegetative medical-cannabis responses to five tested nitrogen supply concentrations under long photoperiod in controlled soilless culture. The reported optimum and deficiency/excess responses are bounded to the studied genotype, stage, environment, medium, nitrogen form, and experimental conditions and are not universal cannabis feed targets.

sources.title: Schwartz and Smart (2024). Abiotic vs. biotic issues in hemp fields.
sources.publisher: Cornell University School of Integrative Plant Science, Cornell Hemp
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for field-level distinction between abiotic disorders and biotic disease in hemp, including spatial-pattern observations and examples of pH, water, temperature, nutrient, wind, and pathogen-associated injury. Symptoms and field patterns are screening evidence, not laboratory confirmation of a causal agent.
sources.reviewUse: hemp diagnostic differential and scouting source

sources.title: Schwartz and Smart (2024). Scouting a hemp field for disease and insects.
sources.publisher: Cornell University School of Integrative Plant Science, Cornell Hemp
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for representative hemp scouting patterns, inspection locations, incidence/severity concepts, spatial records, growth-stage records, and environmental/context observations. Scouting detects and structures evidence; it does not by itself confirm pathogen identity or establish universal action thresholds.

sources.title: Bergstrom, Starr, and Myers (2020). Diseases Affecting Hemp in New York.
sources.publisher: Cornell University School of Integrative Plant Science, Cornell Hemp
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for Cornell-observed hemp disease context in New York, including Botrytis, Septoria and other leaf spots, downy mildew, white mold, seedling/root diseases, and prevention-oriented management. Geographic occurrence, pathogen importance, varietal reaction, and management options are region- and time-dependent; extension observations do not replace causal confirmation for an individual plant.

sources.title: Shiponi and Bernstein (2021). The Highs and Lows of P Supply in Medical Cannabis: Effects on Cannabinoids, the Ionome, and Morpho-Physiology.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for measured medical-cannabis responses across the phosphorus treatments tested in the study, including morphology, ionome and cannabinoid context. Treatment concentrations and response optima are bounded to the studied genotypes, stages, environment and cultivation system and are not universal flowering or fertilizer targets.

sources.title: Toth (2022). Elucidating the Genetic Control of Qualitative Traits in Hemp.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for Cornell hemp-breeding research on molecular markers, cannabinoid chemotype, sex, flowering-time loci Autoflower1 and Early1, photoperiod insensitivity, and marker-assisted selection. Dissertation findings remain bounded to the studied germplasm, populations, marker sets and experiments; they do not establish universal marker performance or inheritance for all Cannabis.
sources.reviewUse: Cornell primary dissertation evidence for hemp genetics and breeding

sources.title: Toth et al. (2022). Flowering Time in Hemp.
sources.publisher: Cornell University School of Integrative Plant Science, Cornell Hemp
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for Cornell extension summary of photoperiod sensitivity, autoflowering material, genetic variation in critical photoperiod, and mapped flowering-time loci in Cornell hemp research. This is a research/extension summary; locus effects and critical photoperiod vary with germplasm and environment and must not be generalized to every Cannabis line.

sources.title: Leyser (2005). The fall and rise of apical dominance.
sources.publisher: Current Opinion in Genetics & Development / PubMed
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for the general plant-development framework of apical dominance, auxin transport, axillary bud outgrowth, and interacting hormonal/nutrient signals. This is general plant biology and does not establish cannabis-specific pruning responses, architecture targets, or yield effects.

sources.title: Finch-Savage and Leubner-Metzger (2006). Seed dormancy and the control of germination.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general seed-dormancy states, environmental sensing, ABA/GA regulation, after-ripening and germination-control concepts. Species-specific dormancy mechanisms vary; this review must not be used to assert a universal Cannabis dormancy class or treatment requirement.

sources.title: Cornell Cooperative Extension. Hardening Transplants.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general transplant hardening principles: gradual acclimation to outdoor light, wind, temperature and water demand before transplanting. This is general horticultural extension guidance and does not establish cannabis-specific hardening duration, transplant timing, or stress thresholds.

sources.title: Petricka, Winter, and Benfey (2012). Control of Arabidopsis root development.
sources.publisher: Annual Review of Plant Biology / PubMed
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for foundational root apical meristem organization, stem-cell niche, cell division, elongation, differentiation and lateral-root developmental concepts. Arabidopsis developmental genetics are a model framework and must not be presented as Cannabis-specific gene regulation or root-zone dimensions.

sources.title: Ruban (2016). Nonphotochemical chlorophyll fluorescence quenching: mechanism and effectiveness in protecting plants from photodamage.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general higher-plant excess-light dissipation, nonphotochemical quenching and photoprotection concepts. This does not establish cannabis seedling PPFD targets, acclimation schedules, or injury thresholds.

sources.title: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic. Root and Crown Rot Diseases.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for university diagnostic context that root/crown decline can involve multiple pathogens and environmental predisposition and requires representative samples and diagnostic confirmation. Clinic guidance is diagnostic framework, not a Cannabis-specific pathogen prevalence or treatment table.

sources.title: Lawson and Blatt (2014). Stomatal size, speed, and responsiveness impact on photosynthesis and water use efficiency.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general relationships among stomatal dynamics, CO2 assimilation, transpiration and water-use efficiency under changing environments. The review is not Cannabis-specific and does not define cultivar-specific conductance, VPD, CO2 or irrigation targets.

sources.title: Kieber and Schaller (2018). Cytokinin signaling in plant development.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for foundational cytokinin biosynthesis/signaling, cell division, shoot development, nutrient signaling and hormone-crosstalk concepts. Model-plant signaling does not establish Cannabis tissue-culture cytokinin recipes, genetic stability, or cultivar-independent response.

sources.title: Buckley (2017). Modeling Stomatal Conductance.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for mechanistic/modeling context connecting stomatal conductance to environmental drivers and transpiration. VPD alone is insufficient to predict whole-crop water loss; model structure, conductance, leaf energy balance and scale matter. Not Cannabis-specific.

sources.title: Shamshiri et al. (2018). Review of optimum temperature, humidity and vapour pressure deficit for greenhouse microclimate evaluation and control.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for greenhouse psychrometric/VPD concepts and the crop/system dependence of microclimate ranges. The reviewed ranges span crops and systems and must not be converted into a universal Cannabis VPD chart.

sources.title: Caplan, Dixon, and Zheng (2019). Increasing Inflorescence Dry Weight and Cannabinoid Content in Medical Cannabis Using Controlled Drought Stress.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for one controlled medical-Cannabis drought-stress experiment and its measured timing/response context. Single-cultivar/system findings do not establish a universal drought recipe, wilt target, cannabinoid response, or safe stress dose.

sources.title: Theocharis, Clément, and Barka (2012). Physiological and molecular changes in plants grown at low temperatures.
sources.useAndLimitations: Use for general chilling/cold effects on membranes, photosynthesis, metabolism, water relations and acclimation. Species and genotype tolerance vary; this review does not establish Cannabis-specific alarm temperatures or cultivar rankings.
